children: AI is changing engineering work faster than traditional career cycles, leaving experienced professionals to confront reskilling, redeployment and the risk that years of expertise may lose relevance

For an engineer, experience has traditionally been an asset that compounds with time. But as artificial intelligence (AI) and automation reshape technical work, a new career risk is emerging: an engineer may still have decades of working life ahead while the skills built over a decade begin losing their commercial value.

This tension is particularly sharp for professionals in the middle of their careers. They command higher salaries and responsibilities, but may also have spent years specialising in technologies or tasks that companies are beginning to redesign. The challenge is therefore not simply whether engineers have jobs, but whether their expertise can remain relevant for the length of their careers.
Experience Meets Disruption
The
NIIT India Skills Gap Report 2026

describes professionals with six to 15 years of experience as both the most sought-after and hardest to replace. Mid-career talent accounts for 47 per cent of recruitment, yet 38 per cent of recruiters identify it as the scarcest talent pool.

The report argues that the constraint is increasingly not hiring but capability progression. Companies need experienced employees, but the value of that experience increasingly depends on whether employees can continuously rebuild their capabilities.
Deloitte’s AI-native workforce: Future of work and skills in engineering and product value chain

, released in February 2026, describes software engineering as moving from creation towards orchestration. The report says GenAI tools can improve new product development times by 50 per cent, while engineering teams have seen productivity gains of 30–40 per cent.
As execution becomes automated, engineering work is shifting toward judgement, architecture, validation, and oversight.

Rajiv C. Mody, CMD and CEO, Sasken Technologies, points to this shift in what engineering expertise itself needs to deliver. “Engineering today is being redefined at a pace we have not seen in decades. The convergence of silicon, software and intelligence is changing not only what engineers can build, but also what is expected of them,” he says.
Mody adds that the engineer of tomorrow will be defined “not simply by the tools they use, but by the judgement they bring to problems that may have no precedent”.
Job Descriptions Change
The transformation is also altering what employers expect from an engineer.

Deloitte’s engineering report says AI is automating routine tasks such as code generation, bug fixes and user-interface scaffolding. Engineers are increasingly expected to guide, validate and integrate AI-generated outputs rather than only produce raw code.

Recruitment is consequently moving from role-based towards capability and skill-based hiring, with AI fluency, adaptability and ethical judgement gaining importance. The report also identifies emerging positions including AI enablement engineers, agent orchestration engineers, context or retrieval engineers and internal developer platform product managers.

This changes the currency of experience. An engineer may have spent a decade mastering a programming language or platform, but the next job could place greater value on supervising AI systems, making architectural decisions and solving problems across technologies.

Ridhima Sawant, Chief Transformation Officer, Orient Technologies, argues that this shift makes judgement increasingly important even as AI accelerates technical execution. “AI can accelerate what we build, but human judgement will continue to define why we build it and the value it creates,” she says.

For engineers trying to remain relevant as technology changes, Sawant also points to continuous learning rather than familiarity with any single technology. “Preparing for this future means more than keeping pace with technology. It means staying curious, learning continuously, experimenting boldly and having the confidence to challenge conventional thinking,” she adds.

Sanjay Agrawal, Head – Presales and CTO, Hitachi Vantara India and SAARC, says this changing environment requires engineers to combine technical expertise with capabilities that extend beyond individual technologies. “This calls for a new generation of engineers who bring together deep technical expertise with cyber resilience awareness, energy efficiency and ethical innovation,” he says.
Reskill Or Replace?
When existing expertise no longer matches emerging requirements, organisations face a difficult choice.
The
NIIT India Skills Gap Report 2026

shows that 69 per cent of organisations increased skills budgets, but 62 per cent said their learning programmes still reached less than half of their workforce. The report also found that 37 per cent of organisations prioritised external hiring, 23 per cent primarily focused on reskilling and 38 per cent balanced the two.

Skill expiry therefore becomes a workforce decision: reskill and redeploy an experienced employee, recruit someone who already has the required capability, outsource the work or automate parts of the role.

But replacing experienced employees can also mean losing years of knowledge about systems, products, customers and operational risks. The challenge is finding a way to acquire current technical capabilities without discarding experience that cannot be quickly recreated.
The Employer Impact
Deloitte’s State of AI in the Enterprise: India Insights, released in April 2026

, found that 32 per cent of surveyed Indian organisations reported extensive job redesign, while another 60 per cent reported moderate redesign. At the same time, 61 per cent were building upskilling or reskilling programmes and 53 per cent were redesigning career paths and building AI fluency.

If jobs themselves are being redesigned, employers must determine where existing employees fit into the new structure. Reskilling too slowly could leave businesses without capabilities required for emerging projects, while repeatedly hiring externally could increase costs and weaken internal career pathways.
The employer challenge is therefore not simply acquiring new skills, but renewing workforce capability without losing valuable experience.

Santana Ramakrishnan, CHRO, ZEISS India, says the changing definition of engineering also places responsibility on organisations to support continuous development. “Engineering is no longer defined only by technical expertise; it is increasingly about the ability to adapt, think critically and apply technology to solve real-world challenges,” she says.
“As AI and emerging technologies reshape the way we work, engineers will need to combine technical knowledge with creativity, collaboration and a continuous learning mindset,” Ramakrishnan adds.
Training Versus Redeployment
There is another gap behind the expansion of corporate learning programmes: completing training does not necessarily mean an employee has successfully changed roles.
An engineer may complete an AI, cloud or data course and still return to the same work. Another may acquire a new capability but find no internal position where it can be applied.

A more revealing measure would be how many mid-career engineers actually move into roles using their newly acquired skills. Whether they retain their grade, compensation and career progression would provide a clearer indication of whether reskilling is protecting careers or simply increasing course-completion numbers.
GCCs Open New Routes
The expansion of Global Capability Centres (GCCs) adds another dimension to the prospects of Indian engineers.

As engineering work moves towards AI-enabled development, platforms and higher-value technology functions, GCC environments can offer opportunities to work on more complex global technology mandates. But the same shift can raise the capability threshold for experienced professionals seeking those roles.

Deloitte’s engineering report notes that South and Southeast Asia are seeing demand for application-based and operational engineering roles, even as engineering functions increasingly require cross-disciplinary capabilities.

For mid-career engineers, GCCs can therefore become both an opportunity and a test. Those who combine domain knowledge with AI, data, cloud, platform or product capabilities may find new routes for progression. Those whose expertise remains concentrated in ageing technologies may find that years of experience alone are no longer enough.
A Career Reset

Even successful reskilling can carry a less visible cost. An engineer who has spent 10 or 12 years becoming an expert may enter a new specialisation alongside professionals with fewer years of experience but deeper knowledge of that technology.

That creates questions around salary, seniority, promotion and internal mobility. Does the engineer retain the value accumulated over the previous decade, or does part of the career effectively reset?

Deloitte’s engineering report says mid-to-senior engineers will increasingly need advanced capabilities to validate AI-generated code, including identifying security flaws and hallucinations. It also sees engineering moving towards design judgement, architectural decisions and end-to-end orchestration.
This suggests experience itself is not becoming obsolete. What is changing is the kind of experience that commands value.

The bigger risk may therefore not be that engineers run out of work, but that the value of what they know changes faster than their careers can adapt. A decade of expertise may still matter, but it may no longer guarantee the next decade of employment.

On Engineers’ Day, that leaves a more uncomfortable question for employers and engineers alike: what happens when an engineer’s expertise reaches its expiry date, but the career built around it is only halfway through?
